title: Calculus I
description: Calculus I develops a unified language for change, approximation, optimization, and accumulation. This syllabus is designed as a rigorous first-semester course that can serve biology, engineering, computer science, economics, chemistry, and mathematics pathways while using discipline-specific applications in problem sets and modeling labs. It emphasizes conceptual understanding, symbolic fluency, numerical reasoning, graphical interpretation, proof-aware theorem use, and clear quantitative communication.

resources.title: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1
resources.description: Best default open textbook. It covers functions, limits, derivatives, and integration with examples and exercises.

resources.title: Calculus: Early Transcendentals
resources.description: James Stewart. Large exercise bank and conventional sequence; useful for engineering-style fluency and homework selection.

resources.title: Thomas' Calculus
resources.description: Clear mainstream reference with strong worked examples and applications.

resources.title: Calculus: Single Variable
resources.description: Hughes-Hallett et al. Especially strong for multiple representations, modeling, and conceptual questions.

resources.title: Calculus (Spivak)
resources.description: Michael Spivak. Optional proof-enrichment text for mathematics majors and advanced students; not the sole text for this mixed audience.

resources.title: Mathematics for Economists
resources.description: Simon and Blume. Optional economics bridge for marginal analysis, optimization, and later multivariable work.

resources.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 18.01SC Single Variable Calculus
resources.description: Self-contained lectures, notes, problem sets, solutions, and challenging exams; the strongest all-in-one open companion.

resources.title: Paul's Online Math Notes - Calculus I
resources.description: Concise explanations and worked problems for quick review and practice.

resources.title: Khan Academy Calculus 1
resources.description: Guided practice and mastery checks for core Calculus I / AP Calculus AB skills.

resources.title: OpenStax student resources
resources.description: Free online reading plus chapter exercises; suitable for an accessible common course baseline.

resources.title: Desmos Graphing Calculator
resources.description: Fast graphing, tables, sliders, numerical roots, and visual checks.

resources.title: GeoGebra Graphing Calculator
resources.description: Interactive graphing and geometry for tangent, accumulation, and optimization explorations.

resources.title: Jupyter
resources.description: Use a spreadsheet or Python/Jupyter for Riemann sums, Newton iterations, numerical integration, data visualization, and reproducible modeling. Require students to explain the mathematics behind any computation.

resources.title: 3Blue1Brown
resources.description: Essence of Calculus: short visual sequence for derivatives, integrals, the chain rule, and the Fundamental Theorem; use for intuition, not as a replacement for problem solving.

resources.title: Professor Leonard
resources.description: Long-form Calculus 1 classroom lectures with detailed examples and pacing suitable for independent review.

resources.title: MIT OpenCourseWare
resources.description: University lectures and problem-solving clips aligned with 18.01SC.

resources.title: The Organic Chemistry Tutor
resources.description: Focused worked examples for common techniques and exam review.

topics.title: Functions, Models, and Multiple Representations
topics.description: Calculus begins with functions: rules that connect changing quantities. This unit aligns algebraic, graphical, numerical, and verbal representations so later derivatives and integrals have meaning rather than becoming isolated procedures.

children.title: Function language and families
children.description: A strong function toolkit lets students recognize structure before calculating. The goal is to see how a formula's form controls its graph, domain, range, and behavior.

children.title: Domain, range, notation, evaluation, and units
Linear, polynomial, rational, power, radical, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric families
Transformations, composition, inverse functions, and piecewise definitions
Zeros, intercepts, symmetry, periodicity, and asymptotic behavior
Representations and modeling
children.description: Real problems rarely arrive as clean formulas. Students learn to translate among data, graphs, equations, and descriptions while stating assumptions and checking units.

children.title: Building a function from a table, graph, verbal rule, or scientific law
Independent and dependent variables; parameters versus variables
Dimensional analysis and unit consistency
Model validity, residual thinking, and limits of extrapolation
Readiness and mathematical communication
children.description: Calculus is easier when algebra and trigonometry are automatic and reasoning is written clearly. This strand diagnoses gaps early and establishes habits used throughout the course.

children.title: Algebraic simplification, factoring, rationalization, and solving equations
Radians, the unit circle, identities, and inverse trigonometric functions
Exact values versus approximations and sensible rounding
Explaining a conclusion with equations, words, graphs, and units

topics.title: Limits and Continuity
topics.description: Limits formalize what a function approaches near a point or far away. They provide the logical foundation for instantaneous rate of change, continuity, asymptotes, and the definite integral.

children.title: Estimating and computing limits
children.description: Students first build intuition from graphs and tables, then develop reliable algebraic techniques. The emphasis is on the behavior near a point, not merely the value at the point.

children.title: Two-sided and one-sided limits from graphs, tables, and formulas
Limit laws and direct substitution
Factoring, rationalizing, common denominators, and trigonometric limits
The Squeeze Theorem and bounding arguments
Infinite behavior and asymptotes
children.description: Limits also describe unbounded growth and long-run behavior. This supports graph analysis and prepares students to reason about scale in scientific and economic models.

children.title: Infinite limits and vertical asymptotes
Limits at infinity and horizontal or slant asymptotes
Dominant-term reasoning for rational and other functions
Distinguishing an infinite limit from a finite limit that fails to exist
Continuity, theorems, and proof awareness
children.description: Continuity captures when small input changes produce small output changes. Students learn the hypotheses and conclusions of key theorems and gain a first, accessible view of epsilon-delta reasoning.

children.title: Continuity at a point and on an interval
Removable, jump, and infinite discontinuities
Intermediate Value Theorem and existence of roots
Epsilon-delta definition: interpreting and constructing simple estimates

topics.title: The Derivative as a Limit and Local Linear Model
topics.description: The derivative measures instantaneous change and gives the best local linear approximation to a differentiable function. This unit connects the geometric tangent, the physical rate, and the analytic limit into one idea.

children.title: From average to instantaneous change
children.description: Secant slopes summarize average change over an interval; a limiting process turns them into tangent slopes and instantaneous rates.

children.title: Average rate of change and difference quotients
Tangent lines, instantaneous velocity, and local rate
Derivative at a point from the limit definition
Units and interpretation of f'(a)
The derivative as a function
children.description: Treating f' as a new function reveals how the original function changes everywhere, not just at a single point.

children.title: Estimating derivative values from data and graphs
Graphing f' from the graph of f and reconstructing qualitative behavior
Differentiability versus continuity; corners, cusps, vertical tangents, and discontinuities
Higher derivatives and changing rates
Linearization and differentials
children.description: A differentiable function behaves nearly linearly at small scales. Linearization turns that insight into a practical approximation and error-estimation tool.

children.title: Tangent-line approximation L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)
Differentials and propagation of small measurement changes
Relative and percentage error
When a local approximation is trustworthy

topics.title: Differentiation Rules and Transcendental Functions
topics.description: Once the derivative is understood as a limit, differentiation rules make it efficient to analyze realistic functions. The aim is fluent computation supported by structural reasoning and quick plausibility checks.

children.title: Core algebraic rules
children.description: The basic rules convert products, quotients, powers, and sums into manageable derivatives while preserving the structure of the original function.

children.title: Constant, power, constant-multiple, sum, and difference rules
Product and quotient rules
Combining rules in multi-step expressions
Checking results by units, signs, special values, or numerical slopes
The chain rule
children.description: Composite functions represent nested processes. The chain rule tracks how change propagates through each layer and is central to science, engineering, economics, and computation.

children.title: Identifying inner and outer functions
Chain rule for algebraic, trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic compositions
Repeated nesting and multiple rule combinations
Sensitivity interpretation through rates multiplied along a dependency chain
Standard transcendental derivatives
children.description: Exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions describe growth, decay, oscillation, rotation, and scaling. Their derivatives make these models analytically useful.

children.title: Derivatives of e^x, a^x, ln(x), and log_a(x)
Derivatives of sine, cosine, tangent, and reciprocal trigonometric functions
Higher-order derivatives and cyclic patterns
Applications to growth, decay, oscillation, and elasticity-like rates

topics.title: Implicit, Inverse, and Logarithmic Differentiation
topics.description: Many important relationships are not solved explicitly for one variable. These techniques extend differentiation to curves, inverse relationships, and complicated products or powers.

children.title: Implicit differentiation
children.description: Implicit differentiation finds rates on a relation F(x,y)=0 without first isolating y, which is often impossible or undesirable.

children.title: Differentiating both sides while treating y as a function of x
Solving for dy/dx and evaluating at a point
Tangent and normal lines to implicit curves
Second derivatives and geometric interpretation
Inverse functions and inverse trigonometric derivatives
children.description: The derivative of an inverse reverses the input-output relationship. This gives a general principle and the formulas for inverse trigonometric functions.

children.title: Conditions for local and global invertibility
Derivative of an inverse function
Derivatives of arcsine, arccosine, arctangent, and related functions
Interpreting reciprocal slopes and domain restrictions
Logarithmic differentiation
children.description: Taking logarithms can turn products into sums and variable powers into products, making otherwise difficult derivatives systematic.

children.title: Products and quotients with many factors
Functions of the form u(x)^v(x)
Absolute values in logarithmic identities where required
Comparing logarithmic differentiation with direct rules

topics.title: Theorems, Curve Analysis, and Indeterminate Forms
topics.description: Derivatives reveal global information about a function when combined with theorem hypotheses. This unit turns local slope data into a disciplined account of extrema, shape, approximation, and limiting behavior.

children.title: Extrema and the Mean Value Theorem
children.description: Existence theorems say when extrema or intermediate slopes must occur. Students learn to check hypotheses before using conclusions.

children.title: Absolute and local extrema; critical numbers and endpoints
Extreme Value Theorem and closed-interval method
Rolle's Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem
Consequences: monotonicity, constant functions, and derivative comparisons
First- and second-derivative analysis
children.description: Sign charts for f' and f'' translate derivative information into a reliable sketch and a qualitative description of behavior.

children.title: Increasing and decreasing intervals
First-derivative test for local extrema
Concavity, inflection points, and the second-derivative test
Complete curve analysis including domain, intercepts, symmetry, and asymptotes
L'Hopital's Rule and approximation behavior
children.description: Indeterminate forms signal competition between quantities. L'Hopital's Rule is useful only after the form and its conditions have been verified.

children.title: Recognizing 0/0 and infinity/infinity forms
Applying L'Hopital's Rule and deciding when to repeat it
Comparing L'Hopital with algebraic, trigonometric, or dominant-term methods
Avoiding misuse when the hypotheses fail

topics.title: Applied Rates, Motion, and Related-Rate Models
topics.description: Calculus becomes powerful when derivatives are attached to quantities with units. This unit develops a repeatable modeling workflow for motion and for systems in which several variables change together.

children.title: Motion and rate interpretation
children.description: Position, velocity, and acceleration provide a concrete setting for first and second derivatives and for interpreting signs and accumulated change.

children.title: Position, displacement, distance, velocity, speed, and acceleration
Units and sign conventions
Reading motion from formulas, graphs, and data
Connecting turning points and concavity to physical behavior
Related-rates workflow
children.description: Related-rates problems test modeling more than algebra. Students identify the governing relation, differentiate before substituting, and interpret the signed result.

children.title: Define variables as functions of time and draw a labeled diagram
Write one relation connecting the changing quantities
Differentiate implicitly with respect to time
Substitute the instant-specific data, solve, and report units
Cross-disciplinary rate models
children.description: A shared calculus structure appears across disciplines even when the vocabulary changes. Problems are selected so every degree sees both familiar and unfamiliar contexts.

children.title: Biology and chemistry: population change, reaction rates, and concentration
Engineering: expanding geometry, fluid levels, heat, motion, and sensor error
Economics: marginal quantities and rates of cost, revenue, and demand change
Computer science: throughput, scaling trends, and continuous approximations to discrete change

topics.title: Optimization and Newton's Method
topics.description: Optimization turns a context into an objective function, a feasible domain, and a justified best choice. Newton's method complements exact analysis with an iterative approach to solving nonlinear equations.

children.title: Optimization modeling
children.description: The central challenge is building the right function and domain. Calculus then identifies candidates, while context decides which candidates are meaningful.

children.title: Objective, decision variables, constraints, and feasible intervals
Reducing a multi-quantity problem to one variable
Critical points, endpoints, and global comparison
Interpreting sensitivity, units, and practical constraints
Discipline-specific optimization
children.description: Different fields ask different questions, but the mathematical architecture is the same: define, differentiate, test, and interpret.

children.title: Engineering design: material, energy, geometry, and performance tradeoffs
Economics: profit, revenue, cost, and elasticity-aware decisions
Biology and chemistry: yield, dose, growth, and reaction conditions
Computing: continuous relaxations of resource and performance choices
Newton's method and numerical roots
children.description: Newton's method uses tangent-line approximations to refine a root estimate. It is a first example of an algorithm whose success depends on both mathematics and initial conditions.

children.title: Deriving x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n) from linearization
Iteration tables and stopping criteria
Convergence, failure, cycling, and poor initial guesses
Comparing Newton's method with graphing and bisection ideas

topics.title: Antiderivatives and Introductory Differential Equations
topics.description: Antidifferentiation reverses differentiation, while differential equations express laws in terms of rates. This unit links families of functions, initial conditions, and simple dynamic models.

children.title: Antiderivatives and indefinite integrals
children.description: Because differentiation loses constants, reversing it produces a family of functions. Students build a compact library of antiderivative patterns.

children.title: Power, exponential, logarithmic, and basic trigonometric antiderivatives
Linearity and algebraic simplification before integration
The constant of integration and families of curves
Checking an antiderivative by differentiation
Initial-value problems
children.description: An initial condition selects one member from an antiderivative family. This provides a direct bridge from rate laws to predictions.

children.title: Recovering position from velocity or acceleration
Solving y' = f(x) with y(a) specified
Interpreting constants from contextual data
Verifying a proposed solution and its units
Simple growth and change models
children.description: Even before a full differential-equations course, students can analyze basic rate models and connect qualitative behavior to a derivative law.

children.title: Constant-rate and proportional-rate models
Exponential growth and decay
Direction-field interpretation at an introductory level
Model assumptions, parameter meaning, and long-run behavior

topics.title: Riemann Sums and the Definite Integral
topics.description: The definite integral measures net accumulation as a limit of many small contributions. Riemann sums make that construction explicit and connect data-based estimates to exact calculus.

children.title: Accumulation from finite sums
children.description: Before taking a limit, students approximate accumulation with rectangles or data intervals and interpret each term as rate times input change.

children.title: Partitions, subinterval width, and sample points
Left, right, midpoint, and general Riemann sums
Sigma notation and dimensional meaning
Overestimates, underestimates, and refinement
The definite integral as a limit
children.description: Letting the mesh width shrink defines a number independent of a particular rectangle choice for integrable functions.

children.title: Limit definition of the definite integral
Signed area and orientation
Basic properties: additivity, linearity, comparison, and bounds
Integrability and the role of continuity
Integral interpretation from graphs and data
children.description: A definite integral is not automatically geometric area; its meaning depends on the integrand and units.

children.title: Net change from a rate graph
Geometric evaluation using familiar shapes and symmetry
Estimating from tabulated measurements
Distinguishing net accumulation from total accumulation

topics.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and Net Change
topics.description: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus unifies the course: differentiation and integration are inverse processes. It turns a limiting sum into a computable quantity and explains accumulation functions.

children.title: Accumulation functions and FTC Part I
children.description: An integral with a variable endpoint defines a new function. Its derivative recovers the original integrand under appropriate conditions.

children.title: Functions defined by accumulated area or net change
Derivative of an integral with a variable upper limit
Chain rule with variable limits
Graphical interpretation of an accumulation function and its derivative
Evaluating definite integrals and FTC Part II
children.description: An antiderivative collapses an infinite limiting process into endpoint subtraction, making exact accumulation practical.

children.title: Evaluation formula F(b) - F(a)
Choosing and verifying an antiderivative
Orientation, interval splitting, and signed results
Units and contextual interpretation
The Net Change Theorem
children.description: Integrating a rate over time gives the change in the original quantity. This principle applies far beyond geometric area.

children.title: Position change from velocity and total distance from speed
Mass, charge, population, concentration, revenue, and cost accumulation
Initial amount plus accumulated change
Average value of a function on an interval

topics.title: Substitution and Applications of Integration
topics.description: Substitution extends the antiderivative toolkit by reversing the chain rule. Applications then use slicing and accumulation to compute areas, volumes, work, and other totals.

children.title: Substitution
children.description: A well-chosen substitution exposes a hidden chain-rule structure and changes both the integrand and, for definite integrals, the bounds.

children.title: Recognizing the inner-function and derivative pattern
Indefinite integrals and back-substitution
Definite integrals with changed bounds
Algebraic, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric examples
Area and volume
children.description: Integration adds infinitely many thin pieces. The hardest step is choosing a slice whose geometry matches the variable of integration.

children.title: Area between curves and intersection points
Volumes by cross-sections and disks/washers
Shell method as an extension when it simplifies geometry
Sketching, bounds, units, and reasonableness checks
Scientific and quantitative applications
children.description: The integral translates a varying density, force, rate, or distribution into a total or average quantity.

children.title: Work from a variable force and basic spring models
Mass from one-dimensional density
Average value and mean behavior
Probability density as enrichment for data-oriented degrees

topics.title: Numerical Integration, Error, and Capstone Modeling
topics.description: Many integrals lack elementary antiderivatives or come only as data. Numerical methods, error awareness, and a final modeling task prepare students to use calculus responsibly in real work.

children.title: Numerical integration
children.description: Numerical rules approximate an integral using function samples. Students compare methods and connect each formula to a geometric picture.

children.title: Left and right sums as baseline methods
Midpoint and trapezoidal rules
Simpson's rule as an enrichment topic
Implementation with a spreadsheet, calculator, or short script
Error and verification
children.description: A numerical answer is incomplete without an estimate of reliability. Students learn to refine, compare, and communicate approximation error.

children.title: Absolute and relative error
Refining the partition and checking stabilization
Qualitative error from monotonicity and concavity
Comparing numerical, graphical, and analytic results
Capstone modeling and communication
children.description: The course culminates in a small, discipline-relevant investigation that combines representation, derivative or integral analysis, computation, and explanation.

children.title: Pose a question and define variables, parameters, units, and assumptions
Choose and justify a model using data or a governing relation
Use derivatives and/or integrals to answer the question
Validate the result, discuss limitations, and present a concise technical narrative
